conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in with a fever and some pain around your central line, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had a fever since they put in that line. It wasn’t supposed to look like this—it was supposed to be a port, but now there’s a tube sticking out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like a Hickman line instead of a port. We’ll check the placement, but the chest X-ray shows it’s in the right spot in your vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I’ve been so tired and achy. Last night I spiked a fever to 103.9. I couldn’t sleep at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been feeling so bad. We’re checking for infections—blood work, urine, and cultures. So far, nothing shows a clear source yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my neck hurts where the line goes in. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s tenderness, but no redness or pus, which is reassuring. We’re watching it closely. We also heard some wheezing—do you have asthma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. It’s been worse the last couple of days. I’ve been coughing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is clear, no pneumonia. But your lungs are tight. We’re going to start you on nebulizers to help with the wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I take something for pain? I just want to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give you your usual hydrocodone for pain. But we’ll monitor your breathing since you’re wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my blood sugar—I’ve been trying to keep it stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 108 when you came in—normal. But we know illness can make it rise. We’ll check it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but still achy. How are the test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are still pending. Urine culture grew some bacteria, but it looks like contamination—probably from vaginal flora.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from the urine. We’re still waiting on blood. But your symptoms—fever, cough, wheezing—suggest a viral bronchitis, possibly triggering your asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been coughing so hard I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense with the coughing. Your abdomen is soft and not tender, so it’s not your chronic pain flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing the nebulizers. And we’d like to start a short course of oral steroids—prednisone—to calm your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? Won’t that mess up my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. That’s why we want to monitor you here. If your sugars go up, we can adjust your insulin. It’s safer than letting the asthma worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that makes sense. But I don’t want to go into DKA again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t let that happen. We’ll check your sugars every few hours and adjust your U500 insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your blood sugar went up to 420 last night after the first steroid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no! Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s high, but you didn’t develop ketones. We increased your U500 insulin under guidance from endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the new dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: 70 units at breakfast, 70 at lunch, and 50 at dinner. We’ll keep checking your sugars to make sure they stay in the 100s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s way more than before. I was only taking 14 units each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because U500 is 5 times stronger than regular insulin. So 70 units of U500 equals about 350 units of regular insulin, which is appropriate with steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. I always get confused with the dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have clear instructions when you go home. Your sugars are already coming down—119 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Less wheezing. You’re responding well to the steroids and nebs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you one more day to make sure your sugars stay stable and you finish a few more doses of steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was thinking of leaving today. I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but with the steroids, your sugars could spike again. And if you go into DKA, it could be serious. Your guardian has been contacted for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be here, but I don’t want to get worse either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just one more night. We’ll keep you comfortable and make sure everything is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood sugars have been in the 100s all night. The endocrine team signed off on your discharge insulin plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever since yesterday. Blood cultures came back negative. We think it was a viral illness, not a line infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow morning. You’ll finish your prednisone at home—7 days total. Keep using your inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin? I’ll need help remembering the new dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a printed sheet. Breakfast and lunch: 70 units of U500. Dinner: 50. Check sugars four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your primary doctor in a week. And please call if you develop fever, trouble breathing, or high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Breathing easier. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember—finish the prednisone, monitor sugars, and care for your line as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—what about the sore throat and those little sores in my mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw the vesicles. They’re likely viral, part of the same illness. They should heal on their own in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was worried it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Just part of what you’ve been through. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. I’m going straight to bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Get some rest. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in follow-up.
